title: A Nice Worksheet
author: Dylan Kane
summary: In his annual 'a nice worksheet' post, math teacher Dylan Kane defends the humble worksheet against its bad reputation and explains what makes a good one. He shares a short fraction-addition worksheet that scaffolds the full procedure after students have practiced each component separately. The anecdote at the center is a struggling student, usually a passive passenger in lessons, who refused to hand in her paper until she finished all eight problems and then asked for another for homework. Kane argues that current curriculum, heavy on word problems and multi-step tasks, often skips the small-step repetitive practice that builds confidence for harder work. He closes with his three basic rules: keep worksheets short, make them accessible with an easy on-ramp, and use just the right amount of repetition, spacing further practice across days.
points: Worksheets earn their bad reputation when they promote passive teaching, but a short, well-built one is among the best tools in a math classroom.
A struggling student who normally disengages became determined to finish because the scaffolded problems made her feel confident and successful.
High standards and rigor are compatible with a little repetitive practice; curriculum heavy on multi-step and analyze-the-mistake problems often skips the confidence-building step.
Kane's rules are brevity (about five minutes of work time), accessibility (an easy first question), and modest repetition spaced across days.
quotes: Worksheets have a bad reputation in math teaching. And for good reason: worksheets can encourage passive teaching.
At a basic level, a worksheet is a piece of paper with math problems on it. That’s probably the best technology we have in a math classroom.
This is a nice worksheet. It breaks a tough topic down into smaller pieces so it’s accessible to students.
But on this day, she was excited to be given something that made her feel confident and successful.
Those are fine, but curriculum often skips the part where we break a concept down into small pieces and give students a little bit of repetitive practice to build confidence for the tough stuff.

A worksheet should also be accessible: every student should be able to get started. That often means the first question or first few questions will be on the simpler side, creating an on-ramp for anything tougher.

There’s more to math class than a piece of paper with eight problems in a row, but often those eight problems in a row build confidence and competence in a way that makes lots of other stuff possible.
